title: Coaching Cut #36: Just-in-Time Feedback
author: Cognitive Coaching
summary: This Coaching Cut explains just-in-time feedback: a coach briefly interrupts a coachee's rehearsal the moment they see modelling slipping back into old patterns, so the coachee recognises the slippage immediately and rehearses correctly within the same session rather than practising the error to fluency. The mechanism respected is motor and cognitive encoding: feedback that waits until the end of a long round lets the coachee install the wrong representation. The piece specifies when to use it (a fundamental misunderstanding only visible once rehearsal begins, or a round long enough that error would compound) and when not to (refinement feedback, which belongs between rounds, or meaty feedback requiring explanation). It should be a small nudge only (pause, reorient, resume), and when several things are wrong the coach should pick one, because correcting one often frees the cognitive capacity for the others to fall into place.
points: Just-in-time feedback briefly interrupts rehearsal to nudge the coachee back toward what was modelled, preventing undesirable habits from encoding.
The mechanism is motor and cognitive encoding: waiting until the end of a long round lets the coachee rehearse and install the wrong action.
Use it when a fundamental misunderstanding surfaces only once rehearsal begins, or when a round is long enough for error to compound.
Do not overuse it, since constant interruption erodes flow and motivation; reserve refinement feedback for between rounds.
When several things are wrong, pick one to correct first, because fixing one often frees cognitive capacity for the others to fall into place.
quotes: Just-in-time feedback is when the coach gives their coachee feedback by briefly interrupting the rehearsal.

where there has been a misunderstanding or a fundamental part of the practice has been forgotten, waiting to give feedback can mean your coachee rehearses wrongly, encoding the wrong actions or choices
Use it when there is a fundamental misunderstanding about the practice the teacher is aiming for and this is only revealed when the teacher starts to rehearse.
If overused, you end up interrupting your coachee's rehearsal too much, which can be demotivating and unproductive.
Often when your coachee corrects one small thing, the others fall into place, or at the very least, your coachee now have the cognitive capacity to address the next one!
